newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW -NZDB has no plans to spin off division.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -NZDB has no plans to spin off division.

text.p: New Zealand Dairy Board chairman Sir Dryden Spring on Tuesday said it had no plans for spinning off its consumer products division as a separate company but remains on the lookout for new brands to buy.
It sees rapid expansion of its branded consumer-pack business, worth NZ$1.2 billion in the May year, as a means of ensuring secure markets for New Zealand's rising milk output.

There have been newspaper reports that turning the consumer products division into a company would be a step towards achieving that expansion, and the board has recently floated the idea in a series of speeches and interviews.
However, Spring told Reuters in an interview: "The board has no plans for floating it as a separate company."

He said the board was constantly looking for opportunities which would expand its value-added business in the increasingly competitive world market. Commodity markets were declining in absolute size and were incapable of absorbing rising milk production, which underlined the need to add value to products.
Buying brands was a central part of that strategy.

"We have already bought a number of brands...Brands give us the opportunity to do two things, firstly, to have secure outlets for New Zealand dairy products, secondly, to have more stable returns and higher returns.

"The price for branded products does not gyrate like the price for traded products. In addition to that, if a brand is strong, is well managed and well supported by technology, significantly higher returns can be obtained," Spring said.
"One of the difficulties we have in buying brands, though, is that most of the business they are used in is business which involves the use of domestically produced milk.

"Few of them provide opportunities for New Zealand imported ingredients to be sold under, but where we can find opportunities that allow us the opportunity to sell additional New Zealand dairy products we are always very keen to take them."
Asked if he could name any brands or companies the board might have earmarked for purchase, Spring replied: "No, I certainly can't do that."
He said the board would not necessarily need foreign equity partners to make further acquisitions, adding that it depended on the size of the opportunity.

"If we were buying a very large brand that may be the case, but by and large the opportunities that we have identified thus far we have been able to accommodate within our normal systems of financing."
The co-operatively owned board had revenue of NZ$5.3 billion in the May year and is one of the world's largest dairy exporters.
Spring saw no sizeable problem in receiving the okay from shareholders on future purchases.

"My experience of this organisation is that sensible propositions will be supported by shareholders. They will put us through a pretty rigorous questioning to be satisfied that the proposals we make are sound, but given that they are sound, our shareholders are most supportive."

Spring said retailer strength was continuing to grow, and in such a climate ensuring products got shelf space meant maintaining a Number One or Number Two brand position. The board is currently a distant third in the international marketplace behind giant multinationals Nestle and Kraft.

Spring said there was no question the board was challenging Nestle and Kraft in certain areas. Asked if the board could be in a position to narrow the gap, however, Spring replied: "I think our businesses are heading in different directions."
